metrics.label: Diesel crack vs Brent

brief.text:
The clearest thing in today's data is that the violence against tankers around the Strait of Hormuz has not stopped. UKMTO reports two tankers attacked in the Strait on Monday 16 November, both with engine-room fires and one left disabled, and a separate report of an LPG tanker (a gas carrier) suffering an engine-room fire after a Hormuz attack, described as at least the 17th reported strike so far in November. If you are fixing Arabian Gulf business, expect owners and their war-risk underwriters — the insurers who cover attack damage — to be cautious on Gulf liftings today.

On prices, note first that no freight index or tanker earnings figure in today's data has refreshed: the Baltic indices are Monday 16 November numbers and the crude tanker earnings are from Sunday 15 November, so nothing can be said about where freight went today. Brent crude is $91.95 a barrel, down 0.5%, and WTI $85.14, down 0.7%, both observed this morning; the data here does not show why. Bunker fuel, the ship's own fuel, moved in opposite directions: VLSFO (low-sulphur fuel oil) in Houston is $755.50 a tonne, up 2.5% today, Rotterdam $748.00 up 0.6% and Fujairah $860.50 up 0.5%, while Singapore slipped 0.5% to $878.00 — again unexplained by today's headlines. For background only, the Baltic Dry Index, which tracks dry bulk cargo rates, stood at 2,921 points on Monday 16 November, and the Baltic Capesize Index — Capesizes being the largest bulk carriers, typically iron ore and coal — at 4,558 on Monday.

Running stories: Hormuz developed clearly today with the two new attacks. The Black Sea also developed — a Somali-flagged cargo ship carrying nearly 3,000 tonnes of wheat capsized off Bulgaria on Monday after a reported sea drone attack, which keeps grain loadings and routing costs in question. Shadow-fleet sanctions moved too: the EU has imposed a new round targeting the shipowners, managers, insurers and financial networks behind Russia's shadow fleet. The Jones Act waiver, US port fees on Chinese-built ships and the Russian diesel export ban had no news in today's data and are unchanged.

What to watch: whether tomorrow's Baltic tanker assessments reflect the Hormuz strikes, and whether charterers and insurers begin re-verifying counterparties after the new EU shadow-fleet designations.

storylines.title: Attacks and blockade enforcement around Hormuz
storylines.what: Attacks on commercial shipping in and around the Strait of Hormuz have continued through November. UKMTO reports two tankers attacked in the Strait on Monday 16 November, both with engine-room fires and one vessel disabled, and an LPG tanker also suffered an engine-room fire after a Hormuz attack.
storylines.why_it_matters: Hull strikes and crew-safety concerns raise war-risk premiums for Arabian Gulf liftings and shrink the pool of willing owners; depressed transit volumes reshape crude and product ton-miles.
storylines.latest: Two further tanker attacks reported in the Strait on 16 November, plus an LPG tanker engine-room fire described as at least the 17th reported strike this month.

storylines.title: Attacks on shipping in the Black Sea and Baltic
storylines.what: Drone strikes on merchant ships in the Black Sea have intensified. A Somali-flagged cargo ship carrying nearly 3,000 tonnes of wheat capsized off Bulgaria on Monday after what crew described as an attack by two sea drones, following earlier strikes near Romania's Sulina anchorage.
storylines.why_it_matters: Strikes on ships and port infrastructure threaten grain and dry bulk loadings and add insurance and routing costs for any vessel calling in the region; proximity to NATO territory widens the risk area.

storylines.title: Sanctions and evasion in the shadow fleet
storylines.what: Sanctions pressure on the shadow fleet is widening. The EU has imposed a new round of measures targeting shipowners, vessel managers, insurers and financial networks supporting Russia's shadow fleet, adding to earlier US designations across Cuban maritime entities and Iranian false-flag registry networks.
storylines.why_it_matters: Designations of managers and insurers force charterers and underwriters to re-verify counterparties, documents and vessel positions, and can strand tonnage outside compliant trade.
storylines.latest: EU announced new sanctions aimed at shadow fleet shipowners, managers and insurers.
sources: EU Targets Shadow Fleet Shipowners, Managers and Insurers in New Russia Sanctions

storylines.title: US Jones Act waiver extended again
storylines.what: A waiver allowing energy companies and traders to move oil, fertilizer and other commodities between US ports on foreign-flagged ships has been extended for another 90 days, with the pause now past 230 days.
storylines.why_it_matters: The waiver keeps foreign-flag tonnage eligible for US coastwise cargoes, affecting demand for US-flag ships and the employment of product tankers in domestic trades.

storylines.title: US Jones Act waiver extended again
storylines.what: A waiver allowing energy companies and traders to move oil, fertilizer and other commodities between US ports on foreign-flagged ships has been extended for another 90 days, with the pause now past 230 days.
storylines.why_it_matters: The waiver keeps foreign-flag tonnage eligible for US coastwise cargoes, affecting demand for US-flag ships and the employment of product tankers in domestic trades.
sources: New US Policy Priorities Could Shape Future Shipping Markets

storylines.title: Russian diesel flows and export restrictions
storylines.what: A reported US-Russia arrangement on extra diesel for the US market has met political opposition, while Russia has extended a ban on most diesel exports to end-January.
storylines.why_it_matters: Diesel export restrictions and any reopened Atlantic route reshape clean product tanker ton-miles and MR and LR employment.
sources: EU Targets Shadow Fleet Shipowners, Managers and Insurers in New Russia Sanctions

storylines.title: US port fees on Chinese-built and Chinese-operated ships
storylines.what: The US administration has formally extended its suspension of port fees targeting Chinese-built and Chinese-operated vessels for another two months while trade talks continue.
storylines.why_it_matters: The fees, if reinstated, would change the cost of deploying Chinese-built tonnage into US trades and affect chartering preferences across sectors.
sources: New US Policy Priorities Could Shape Future Shipping Markets
